notes.shape: A yield curve plots Treasury yields across maturities from 1 month to 30 years, with a normal upward slope indicating higher yields for longer maturities. An inverted slope, where shorter-term yields exceed longer-term yields, has historically preceded US recessions by 6 to 18 months. Currently, the 10-year Treasury yield stands at 4.71% for June 2026, with the 10-year minus 2-year (2s10s) spread at 0.36 percentage points, indicating a positively sloped curve. This marks a shift from the 2022-2024 period when the curve experienced inversion, as the spread had dropped to 0.0 points, the deepest inversion recorded in this series.
notes.signal: The 2s10s spread serves as a key recession indicator; an inversion (spread below zero) has historically foreshadowed recessions. After spending 2022-2024 inverted, the spread has re-steepened above zero to 0.36 points, suggesting easing recession concerns. However, the New York Fed's recession probability remains at 31%, a non-negligible risk level. It is important to note that the curve often reverts to a positive slope—un-inverts—shortly before a recession begins, which can temper interpretations of the current positive spread.
notes.now: Currently, the yield curve's positive slope and the 0.36-point 2s10s spread indicate reduced immediate recession risk compared to the recent inversion period. Nevertheless, the elevated 31% recession probability from the NY Fed suggests cautious monitoring remains warranted without a definitive timing signal.
